entry: American psychologist, behaviorist and social philosopher. He founded the experimental analysis of behavior, a school of experimental research [[Psychology|psychology]], and developed the philosophy of radical [[Behaviorism]]. Skinner used operant conditioning to strengthen behavior and considered the rate of response the most effective measure of response strength. To study it he invented the operant conditioning chamber, known as the Skinner box, and the cumulative recorder. With Charles Ferster he produced his most influential experimental work, outlined in *Schedules of Reinforcement* (1957). He was Edgar Pierce Professor of Psychology at [[Harvard University]] from 1948 until his retirement in 1974. His utopian novel *Walden Two* (1948) envisioned a community designed on his ideas, and *Verbal Behavior* (1958) analyzed human behavior. Critics, including [[Noam Chomsky]], challenged the application of operant principles to language. A June 2002 survey listed him as the most influential psychologist of the 20th century.

Indian jurist, economist, politician and social reformer. Born in Mhow, now in Madhya Pradesh, into a Mahar caste treated as untouchable, he studied economics at [[Columbia University]] and the [[London School of Economics]]. At Columbia he came under the influence of [[John Dewey]] and his philosophy of pragmatism. He chaired the drafting committee of the [[Constitution of India]], which was based on the debates of the Constituent Assembly and an earlier draft by Sir Benegal Narsing Rau, and he served as law and justice minister in the first cabinet of [[Jawaharlal Nehru]]. He campaigned for political rights and social freedom for [[Dalit|Dalits]]. He renounced [[Hinduism]] and in 1956 converted to [[Buddhism]], initiating mass conversions of Dalits. The Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, was conferred on him posthumously in 1990.

Hungarian composer. He is considered one of the most important composers of the 20th century, and with [[Franz Liszt]] he is regarded as Hungary's greatest composer. Through his collection and analysis of [[Folk music|folk music]], he was one of the founders of comparative musicology, later known as ethnomusicology. His early work was influenced by [[Richard Strauss]] and [[Johannes Brahms]], and from 1907 he came under the influence of [[Claude Debussy]]. His mature style blended peasant folk music with modernist techniques. He studied at the Royal Academy of Music in [[Budapest]], and his works include the opera *Bluebeard's Castle*, the ballet *The Miraculous Mandarin*, *Music for Strings, Percussion and Celesta* and six string quartets. In 1940 he emigrated to the United States, where he continued research at [[Columbia University]].

King of Hungary and Croatia (r. 1235–70). The eldest son of King Andrew II, Béla was crowned in his father's lifetime, in 1214, and governed [[Transylvania]] as duke from 1226. He supported Christian missions among the pagan [[Cumans]], and some Cuman chieftains acknowledged his suzerainty; he adopted the title King of Cumania in 1233. After the [[Mongols]] annihilated his army at the Battle of Mohi on April 11, 1241, and devastated the country until their withdrawal in March 1242, he introduced reforms to prepare for a second invasion. He allowed barons and prelates to build stone fortresses, promoted fortified towns, and welcomed colonists from the [[Holy Roman Empire]] and neighboring regions to resettle depopulated lands. These efforts earned him the epithet "second founder of the state." He was duke of Styria from 1254 to 1258. A dispute with his son Stephen led to civil war until 1266.

Vietnamese staple food, a short baguette with a thin, crisp crust and soft interior, usually made from mixed rice and [[Wheat|wheat]] flour. Often split lengthwise and filled with meat, pickled carrots and daikon, cilantro, [[Mayonnaise|mayonnaise]] and [[Chili pepper|chili]], it is served as a meal or eaten plain. The baguette was introduced by the French colonial administration in the mid-19th century. In the 1950s a distinctly Vietnamese sandwich developed in Saigon, and after the [[Vietnam War]] overseas Vietnamese popularized it in countries such as Australia, Canada and the United States.

Jewish mystic and healer regarded as the founder of [[Hasidic Judaism]]. A *baal shem tov*, or "Master of the Good Name," was one able to work miracles using a secret name of God. A central tenet of his teaching was *devekut*, a direct connection with the divine infused in every human activity and waking hour. Prayer was of supreme importance. Biographical information comes from documents of the [[Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth]], including a census entry for a holy man in Medzhybizh from 1740 to 1760, presumably him, and from legends collected in *Praise of the Besht* (*Shivḥei haBesht*). Several letters attributed to him were printed after his death, but scholars debate their authenticity.

Northwest Semitic title meaning "owner" or "lord," later applied to gods. The name was particularly associated with the storm and fertility god Hadad, and Baal was linked to rain, lightning, wind and kingship. Worship spread throughout the [[Levant]]. The Ugaritic Baal is the protagonist of the *Baal Cycle*, one of the lengthiest surviving epics of the ancient Near East. The [[Hebrew Bible]] portrays Baal as a foreign or rival deity opposed by the prophet [[Elijah]], and the [[Quran]] likewise presents him as a false god.

Witchlike figure from Slavic folklore, sometimes one of three sisters who share the name. In some narratives she is a repulsive old woman who fries and eats children, while in others she is a kindly figure who helps the hero, and both versions often depict her as a witch. She is often associated with forest wildlife. Her distinctive traits are flying in a wooden mortar, wielding a pestle, and living deep in the forest in a [[Hut|hut]] with chicken legs. In many [[Slavic languages]], *baba* means "grandmother" or "old woman," but the origin of *yaga* is unclear and has no scholarly consensus. The first clear reference to her appears in Mikhail V. Lomonosov's *Russian Grammar* of 1755.

Iranian revolutionary leader in the Khorramdin rebellion against the [[Abbasid Caliphate]]. The movement took its name from *Khorram-Dinān* ("Those of the joyous religion"), which is considered an offshoot of neo-Mazdakism. Based in [[Azerbaijan]] in northwestern [[Iran]], Babak's rebellion called for a return to the political glories of the Iranian past. It spread to western and central Iran and lasted more than twenty years until Babak was betrayed and defeated. Sources give conflicting accounts of his origins; his original name was al-Hasan, and he probably adopted the name Babak near the start of his rebellion. The uprising showed the continuing strength of ancestral Iranian local feelings in the region.

American golfer and athlete. At the 1932 [[Olympic Games|Summer Olympics]] in Los Angeles she won gold in the 80-meter hurdles, in 11.7 seconds, and in the javelin throw, with an Olympic record of 43.69 meters, and she took silver in the high jump. She set four world records at those Games and became the first woman to win more than one event at a single Olympic Games. She was also a three-time AAU All-American in [[Basketball|basketball]] from 1930 to 1932 and played organized [[Baseball|baseball]] and softball. She was also a singer and [[Harmonica|harmonica]] player who recorded several songs on the Mercury Records label. After turning to professional golf she won 10 LPGA major championships.

American baseball player, nicknamed "the Bambino" and "the Sultan of Swat." He spent 22 seasons in [[Major League Baseball]], from 1914 through 1935. He began as a left-handed pitcher for the [[Boston Red Sox]] and was a member of three [[World Series]] championship teams with them before becoming a slugging outfielder. In 1919 he broke the single-season home run record with 29 and was sold to the [[New York Yankees]] after that season amid controversy. With the Yankees he helped win seven American League pennants and four World Series championships. He hit 60 home runs in 1927 as part of the "Murderers' Row" lineup. He led the American League in home runs 12 times and was elected to the [[Baseball]] Hall of Fame in 1936 as one of its "first five" members.

Genus of [[Old World monkey|Old World monkeys]] in the family Cercopithecidae. Its six species, the hamadryas, Guinea, olive, yellow, Kinda and chacma baboons, are each native to one of six areas of [[Africa]], and the hamadryas also to part of the [[Arabian Peninsula]]. Baboons are among the largest non-hominoid [[Primate|primates]] and have existed for at least two million years. The Kinda baboon, the smallest, is 50 cm long and weighs 14 kg; the chacma, the largest, reaches 120 cm and 40 kg. Males and females show [[Sexual dimorphism|sexual dimorphism]] in size, color and canine development. Baboons are diurnal and sleep in trees or on cliffs at night, away from predators such as [[Leopard|leopards]], [[Lion|lions]] and [[Hyena|hyenas]]. Most live in hierarchical troops containing harems, and females usually remain in their birth group for life. In captivity they live up to 45 years; in the wild, 20 to 30.

Founder of the [[Mughal Empire]] in South Asia (r. 1526–1530). A descendant of [[Timur]] through his father and of [[Genghis Khan]] through his mother, Babur was born in Andijan in the Fergana Valley, now in Uzbekistan. He lost and regained [[Samarkand]] several times before taking [[Kabul]] in 1504. He then turned to India, and at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 he defeated Ibrahim Lodi, the sultan of Delhi. At the Battle of Khanwa his troop positioning and use of gunpowder brought victory over a coalition led by Rana Sanga. He wrote the *Baburnama* in Chaghatai Turkic, which was translated into Persian during the reign of his grandson [[Akbar]]. He was first buried in [[Agra]], but his remains were moved to Kabul as he wished. His son [[Humayun]] succeeded him.

Demographic cohort, often defined as people born from 1946 to 1964, that followed the [[Silent Generation]] and preceded [[Generation X]]. The cohort was born in the mid-20th-century baby boom that followed World War II. Boomers grew up during Cold War education reforms and economic prosperity. As young people they created social movements and a distinctive rhetoric around their generation, which shaped public perception of the cohort and popularized generational thinking. Most boomers are parents of Generation X and [[Millennials]]. In the United States they remain the second-largest age demographic, after millennials.

American space opera television series. Created by J. Michael Straczynski, it premiered on January 26, 1994, and ran for five seasons of 22 episodes. It follows human and alien characters on a [[Space station|space station]] built after several interspecies wars as neutral ground for galactic diplomacy and trade. It was conceived as a "novel for television" with a pre-planned five-year story arc, unusual for American broadcast television at the time. The human characters become pivotal to resistance against Earth's descent into [[Totalitarianism|totalitarianism]]. A reboot was announced in September 2021.

Ancient city on the [[Euphrates|Euphrates]] River in southern [[Mesopotamia]], in present-day [[Iraq]]. Babylon was the main cultural and political centre of [[Babylonia]] and the capital of the Old Babylonian Empire, founded in the 18th century BC by [[Hammurabi]], and of the Neo-Babylonian Empire from 626 to 539 BC. It has been estimated to have been the largest city in the world around c. 1770–c. 1670 BC and again around c. 612–c. 320 BC. The Hanging Gardens and walls of Babylon were ranked among the [[Seven Wonders of the Ancient World|Seven Wonders of the Ancient World]], although some scholars question whether the gardens existed. [[UNESCO]] recognized Babylon as a [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]] in 2019, but local construction threatens to encroach upon the ruins.

Ancient Akkadian-speaking state centered on the city of [[Babylon]] in central-southern [[Mesopotamia]], in present-day [[Iraq]] and parts of [[Syria]]. It emerged around 1894 BC as an Akkadian-populated state ruled by Amorites. Under [[Hammurabi]] it briefly became the major power in the region, but the empire fell apart rapidly after his death. Babylonia often rivaled [[Assyria]] to the north and [[Elam]] to the east. It retained Akkadian as its written language for official use, while Sumerian remained in sacred texts for the Babylonian religion. The region stayed an important cultural centre even under long periods of outside rule.

Period of Jewish exile in [[Babylonia]] during the 6th century BCE. [[Nebuchadnezzar II]] deported Judeans from the Kingdom of Judah in waves: about 7,000 after the siege of [[Jerusalem]] in 597 BCE, and more after the city and its temple were destroyed in 587 BCE. After the Persians took Babylon in 539 BCE, [[Cyrus the Great]] permitted exiles to return, but a sizable Jewish community persisted in Mesopotamia. Its descendants are believed to form the ancestry of the Iraqi, Persian, Georgian, Bukharian and Mountain Jewish communities.

Comparing card game between two hands, the "player" and the "banker." Now played mainly in [[Casino|casinos]], it has origins in precursors from China, Japan and Korea, and it gained popularity in Europe, where a faster French variant emerged. The most common version today is of Cuban origin. Each round has three possible outcomes: player, banker or tie. The bank has the winning odds, with a house edge of at least one percent.

Undergraduate degree awarded by higher education institutions after a course of study lasting three to six years. The two most common are the Bachelor of Arts (BA) and the Bachelor of Science (BS or BSc). The term derives from Medieval Latin *baccalaureus*; in the 12th century *bachelor* referred to a young or poor knight. Systems influenced by Britain distinguish honours degrees, which generally require a higher academic standard, from non-honours pass or general degrees. Australia, New Zealand, South Africa and [[Canada|Canada]] also offer a postgraduate "bachelor with honours" degree, which typically requires a full year-long research thesis. Completion of a bachelor's degree is usually a prerequisite for a [[University|university]] master's or doctorate.

1985 American science fiction film directed by [[Robert Zemeckis]]. [[Michael J. Fox]] plays Marty McFly, a teenager accidentally sent from 1985 to 1955 in a [[Plutonium|plutonium]]-powered DeLorean time machine built by his scientist friend Emmett "Doc" Brown. Its release was brought forward to July 3, 1985, and it became the highest-grossing film of 1985 worldwide. It won an Academy Award, and in 2007 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry. Two sequels followed, *Back to the Future Part II* (1989) and *Back to the Future Part III* (1990), and [[Universal Pictures]] launched a multimedia franchise.

Two-player [[Board game|board game]] played with counters and dice. It is the most widespread Western member of the tables family, whose ancestors date back at least 1,600 years. Each player has 15 pieces, traditionally called men, which move along 24 points according to the roll of two dice. The objective is to move all of one's pieces around the board and bear them off first. Removing all pieces while the opponent is still far behind earns a triple win, known as a backgammon. The game combines strategy with luck, and a doubling cube lets players raise the stakes during play. The earliest record of backgammon itself dates to 17th-century England, where it descended from the 16th-century game of Irish.

American pop vocal group and boy band, often abbreviated BSB. Formed in [[Orlando, Florida|Orlando]] in 1993, the group comprised Nick Carter, Howie Dorough, AJ McLean, Brian Littrell and Kevin Richardson. Its album *Millennium* (1999), anchored by the hit "I Want It That Way," brought worldwide success. The group has sold over 150 million records, making it the best-selling boy band of all time. It was the first group since [[Led Zeppelin]] to have its first ten albums reach the top 10 on the Billboard 200. It received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 2013.

Salt-cured [[Pork|pork]] made from the belly or less fatty parts of the back. It is eaten as a side dish, especially at [[Breakfast|breakfast]], used as a central ingredient in the BLT [[Sandwich|sandwich]], or used as a flavoring. Bacon is also used to wrap and lard roasts, especially game such as venison and pheasant. The word derives from Proto-Germanic *bakkon*, meaning "back meat." Curing typically uses salt and often [[Sodium nitrite|sodium nitrite]], followed by smoking or cooking. Meat from beef, lamb, chicken or turkey may be prepared to resemble bacon, and vegetarian versions such as "soy bacon" exist. Because of its high fat and sodium content, it is classified as a processed meat, and dietary guidelines recommend moderation.

Ancient civilization and region in Central Asia, between the [[Hindu Kush]] to the south and the [[Amu Darya|Amu Darya]] to the north, largely within modern Afghanistan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. In the Zoroastrian faith it is one of the "sixteen perfect Iranian lands," and it was an early centre of [[Zoroastrianism]]. Bactria became a satrapy of the [[Achaemenid Empire]], ruled by a crown prince, and it resisted Greek Macedonian invaders before falling to [[Alexander the Great]]. After his death it passed to the [[Seleucid Empire]], but the satrap Diodotus I declared independence, beginning the Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek kingdoms. The [[Parthian Empire]] conquered Bactria in the 2nd century BC, and the [[Kushan Empire]] in the early 1st century. Bactrian, an Eastern Iranian language, was the common language until early medieval times.
